raw_case_text:
This 53-year lifelong nonsmoker lady presented with acute onset pleuritic chest pain, and shortness of breath started a few hours before hospital attendance. The patient denies cough, sputum production, haemoptysis, or other respiratory symptoms at the time of presentation. There were no constitutional symptoms, namely, loss of weight, poor appetite, fever, or excess sweating. Importantly, no family history of asthma, malignancy, or venous thrombosis was noted. She does not keep pets at home.
Clinical examination at the A/E showed normal vital signs apart from a respiratory rate of 20 cycles per minute. There were reduced chest expansion and reduced breath sound on chest examination. Other system examinations were unremarkable.
Laboratory tests showed peripheral eosinophilia with absolute count 1.0 K/mul (0.8) representing 16%, elevated CRP of 13 mg/dl, and ESR of 60 mm/hr. Her CXR showed bilateral opacities over the right middle and left lower zones (Figure 1). The D-dimer was also raised (0.72 mug/ml FEU). Because of acute presentation of pleuritic chest pain with shortness of breath and elevated D-dimer, the team requested CTPA, which was negative for pulmonary embolism but showed soft tissue density masses in both the right and left lungs (Figure 2).
Initially, she was managed with intravenous levofloxacin, bronchodilator, analgesia, and prophylactic anticoagulation by A/E colleges and later referred to our respiratory team as a case of possible lung mass for bronchoscopy.
On further questions, she gave a previous history of intermittent shortness of breath with a wheezy chest triggered by dust and smoke. Moreover, she had a medical review twice and responded to nebulized bronchodilators. Yet, she was never prescribed long-term inhalers.
Flexible bronchoscopy was performed, which illustrated a whitish, cheesy, and very viscid mucous plug. It was challenging when attempting suction (Figure 3). The eosinophil count was 9%, and segmented neutrophils were 68% on bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL). The BAL cultures grew Streptococcus pneumoniae and Aspergillus species (not determined). Other tests were negative, including cytology and acid-fast bacilli stain and cultures.
In view of asthma-like symptoms, peripheral eosinophilia, radiological changes, and mucous plug, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis was suspected. Therefore, we requested total IgE level and Aspergillus-specific IgE. Empirical treatment with methylprednisolone 40 mg daily was initiated for presumable diagnosis of ABPA, awaiting laboratory confirmation.
Later, results came with a total IgE of more than 5000 IU/ml, Aspergillus fumigatus IgE of 19.6 kU/l (elevated), and Aspergillus niger IgE of 52.8 kU/l (elevated).
We discharged her on oral prednisolone 40 mg daily and a plan to taper down gradually in addition to asthma management with a salbutamol inhaler when needed (budesonide/formoterol 160/4.5 mcg turbuhaler twice daily and montelukast 10 mg tablet once daily).
Two weeks later, her symptoms resolved, and a chest X-ray showed the resolution of previously seen bilateral opacities.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 53-year-old lifelong non-smoking woman presented with acute-onset pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath that began a few hours prior to emergency department arrival.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the emergency department with sudden-onset pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea of a few hours' duration without cough or fever. Although CT pulmonary angiography excluded pulmonary embolism, it revealed bilateral lung masses. Upon detailed respiratory inquiry, she disclosed a prior history of intermittent wheezing and dyspnea triggered by dust and smoke that had responded to nebulized bronchodilators on two prior occasions without maintenance inhaler therapy.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of uninvestigated intermittent dust- and smoke-triggered wheezing and dyspnea responsive to nebulized bronchodilators; lifelong non-smoker; no household pets; no family history of asthma, malignancy, or venous thromboembolism.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for acute pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath; negative for current cough, sputum, hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, anorexia, or weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: Vital signs were normal except for mild tachypnea (respiratory rate 20 breaths/min). Chest examination revealed reduced chest expansion and diminished breath sounds; other systemic examinations were normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed peripheral blood eosinophilia (absolute eosinophil count 1.0 K/uL [16%]; reference <0.8 K/uL), elevated CRP (13 mg/dL), elevated ESR (60 mm/h), and mildly elevated D-dimer (0.72 ug/mL FEU). Subsequent immunologic testing revealed markedly elevated total serum IgE (>5,000 IU/mL), elevated Aspergillus fumigatus-specific IgE (19.6 kU/L), and elevated Aspergillus niger-specific IgE (52.8 kU/L). Chest X-ray showed bilateral opacities in the right middle and left lower zones (which resolved completely after 2 weeks of prednisolone).
objective.advanced_workup: CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) was negative for pulmonary embolism but demonstrated bilateral soft-tissue-density lung masses (mucoid impaction). Flexible bronchoscopy revealed a thick, whitish, cheesy, highly viscid mucus plug that was difficult to suction; bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) differential showed 9% eosinophils and 68% segmented neutrophils (negative for malignant cytology and AFB), and BAL cultures grew Aspergillus species and Streptococcus pneumoniae.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) presenting with acute pleuritic chest pain and bilateral pseudotumoral mucoid impaction in a patient with undiagnosed bronchial asthma, confirmed by peripheral eosinophilia (16%, 1.0 K/uL), total serum IgE >5,000 IU/mL, elevated specific IgE to Aspergillus fumigatus (19.6 kU/L) and Aspergillus niger (52.8 kU/L), and bronchoscopic visualization and BAL culture of viscid eosinophilic mucus plugs growing Aspergillus sp. Treated with intravenous methylprednisolone (40 mg/day) transitioned to a tapering course of oral prednisolone (40 mg/day) alongside inhaled budesonide/formoterol (160/4.5 ug twice daily), montelukast (10 mg daily), and as-needed salbutamol, achieving complete clinical and chest X-ray resolution within 2 weeks.
